description: Inspired by forensic accountants' use of Benford's law, including Mark Nigrini's work and cases such as the 1993 Arizona state-treasury cheque fraud, where invented amounts avoided low leading digits. The Hampi crew's 248 claims were invented. Their sizes match the other crews category by category, but their leading digits are spread almost evenly: only about 13% start with 1, against about 30% expected, and 8s and 9s are two to three times too common. Tabulate the first digit of amount_inr for each crew and compare it with Benford's log10(1 + 1/d). Hampi's deviation is several times larger than any other crew's.
hints: Averages, medians and category totals all look reasonable. Real money leaves a subtler fingerprint than its size. Look at how the amounts are written, digit by digit.
Take the leading digit of every amount_inr and compare its distribution, separately for each crew, with Benford's law: about 30% of amounts should start with 1 and under 5% with 9.
One crew's leading digits are almost flat. Only about 13% of Hampi's claims start with 1, and 8s and 9s are two to three times too common. The Hampi crew invented its claims.
